events.name: History Film Forum presents "Faith Healers"
events.description: The History Film Forum proudly presents Faith Healers , in partnership with the Smithsonian Asian Pacific American Center. Faith Healers explores the history of doctors who left the Philippines to care for patients in the United States. The documentary traces Dr. Zorayda Lee-Llacer's journey to the United States and her contributions to American healthcare. Against the backdrop of the colonial relationship between the United States and the Philippines, the film examines the challenges and achievements of a vibrant Filipino American community that grew just outside the nation’s capital in Prince George’s County, Maryland. Along with the story of Dr. Lee-Llacer, the film explores the experiences of second-generation Filipino Americans and examines how the Philippines continues to shape their identities from afar. Faith Healers is ultimately a story of sacrifice, service, community, and the preservation of Filipino American history. After the screening, enjoy a panel conversation with: Regina Aquino (writer, director, and executive producer of Faith Healers ) Dr. Zorayda M. Lee-Llacer (physician) Professor Erwin R. Tiongson (Professor and Director of the Global Human Development Program, Georgetown University) Moderator: Ryan Lintelman (curator, National Museum of American History) The National Museum of American History welcomes visitors of all ages and abilities. This event is wheelchair accessible. Captioning and assistive listening devices will be provided. Additional accommodations are available upon request; please email nmahprograms@si.edu . Two weeks’ notice is preferred. Seating is limited and reservations are recommended. Seating will be opened first to Eventbrite-registered attendees and then to walk-in visitors. When we reach maximum capacity, the event will be closed to the public.

events.name: Broad Stripes and Bright Stars
events.description: Meet Mary Pickersgill, seamstress of the enormous garrison flag that inspired the lyrics to America’s national anthem and later became known as the Star-Spangled Banner. What was it like to live in a nation defending its sovereignty? Learn about the War of 1812, considered America’s Second War of Independence, and about ways that widows like Mary expressed patriotism and resourcefulness through acquired skills and family connections.

events.name: Go-Go Fitness
events.description: Join Go-Go Fitness LLC as they lead a fun dance fitness workshop for the whole family to DC’s home sound – Go-Go Music. Dress in loose fitting, comfortable clothes, wear tennis shoes, and bring water and a hand towel. Reserve your spot today! Since February 2012, Go-Go Fitness LLC has been a trusted partner and leader in dance fitness and total health and wellness in the District, the nation and the world spreading the love of DC’s homegrown Go-Go Music through dance fitness. Native Washingtonians Danette Tucker and Erica Berry Wilson started Go-Go Fitness to provide a family-friendly environment that encourages women, men and children of all ages to get fit and have fun while doing so. Throughout our history, we have encouraged physical activity to support the health and well-being of families and communities.

events.name: Teen Studio: Are You Surreal?
events.description: Teens: Ready to level up your art? Join us for Teen Studio, a free art-making program exclusively for teens ages 13–19. Push your artistic boundaries using materials and techniques inspired by artists whose work is now on view at the Hirshhorn. Think like a Surrealist! This Saturday, check out Moonmad by Max Ernst, a surrealist piece that blurs a recognizable face into something totally dream-like. Then head back to Art School to explore portraiture as a tool for self-expression, experimentation, and storytelling with guest artist Simone Agoussoye. Guest Artist Simone Agoussoye Simone Agoussoye is a Washington, D.C.-born multidisciplinary artist, curator, and arts educator whose work explores identity, visibility, self-worth, and the experiences of Black women through portraiture. Known for incorporating materials such as broken and crushed glass into her work, Agoussoye uses texture, reflection, and light to expand traditional approaches to portraiture. She has exhibited throughout the DMV and beyond and has spent the past six years teaching and facilitating arts programming for young people, including students at Washington School for Girls and through George Washington University’s community arts programming. Drop in to Teen Studio every Saturday between 2:30 and 4:30 PM. Register for the entire school year here (one-time registration covers all sessions). Join one session or join them all! Meet in Art School on the Museum’s Lower Level. Looking for more? Explore Art School Everywhere , wherever you are, to learn about artists in the Hirshhorn collection and get creative any time. Do this at home! Do this at home! Picasso Rocks! Pablo Picasso. Bust of a Woman (Dora Maar) , 1938. Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC, Gift of Joseph H. Hirshhorn, 1966 ABOUT TEEN STUDIO Teens ages 13–19 are invited to hang out and get creative at the Hirshhorn’s Teen Studio . Teen Studio is a free series of art-making workshops offered from 2:30 to 4:30 PM every Saturday. All skill levels are welcome—from the novice notebook doodler to the experienced teen artist, there’s something for everyone! Each month, we’ll dive into a fresh theme inspired by artists on view. Each workshop will offer a mix of time in the galleries, where we’ll encounter groundbreaking artists, and time in Hirshhorn Art School, where we’ll experiment with new media and materials. Whether you’re into painting, sculpture, 3D design, animation, or something else, you’ll get hands-on experience and unlock new creative skills. If there are services or accommodations that can improve your experience (e.g., ASL interpretation, live captioning, etc.), please contact HMSGEducation@si.edu . We appreciate receiving such requests at least one to two weeks in advance.

events.name: Virtual Book Club | Martyr! by Kaveh Akbar
events.description: Register to join. Halloween costumes welcome~ Calling all readers! We’re starting a quarterly virtual book club, hosted by NPR’s Emily Kwong. You may recognize her from the hit podcast Inheriting about AAPI family history. Our club will meet once each season, with fresh recommendations from some of our favorite Asian-owned bookstores (including Loyalty Bookstore and Yu & Me Books). Expect: open-ended questions, organic conversation, and a structured activity. To kick off the club, our first book is Martyr! by Kaveh Akbar. Grab a copy from the museum store on your next visit. About Martyr! A newly sober, orphaned son of Iranian immigrants, guided by the voices of artists, poets, and kings, embarks on a remarkable search for a family secret that leads him to a terminally ill painter living out her final days in the Brooklyn Museum. Electrifying, funny, and wholly original, Kaveh Akbar’s debut novel is a paean to how we spend our lives seeking meaning—in faith, art, ourselves, others. Martyr! is a New York Times bestseller, National Book Award finalist, one of The New York Times Book Review ’s 10 Best Books of 2024, and a TIME Must-Read Book of 2024. “Kaveh Akbar is one of my favorite writers. Ever.“—Tommy Orange, Pulitzer Prize–nominated author of There There “ Martyr! is nothing short of miraculous.“— The New York Times Book Review Synopsis adapted from Penguin Random House. Meet Your Host Emily Kwong Emily Kwong (she/her) is an NPR audio journalist working at the crossroads of history, science, and family memory. She is the host of two shows: Short Wave , NPR’s science podcast, and Inheriting , LAist’s show about Asian American and Pacific Islander families. Her reporting style is driven by empathy and context—rooted in a sense of people’s lives continuing on long after the story ends. Season 2 of Inheriting will debut in January 2027 and is about five families shaped by five immigration policies passed down through the generations. You can find her on Instagram @kwongsong. Emily loves to curl up with a good book and her orange cat Zuko. She’s very excited to host the first ever virtual book club for the National Museum of Asian Art. Book cover courtesy of Penguin Random House.

events.name: DC | Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead)
events.description: Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) is a time for commemorating our ancestors. Rather than a period of mourning, it is an occasion for celebrating with family—both living and dead—and honoring the cycle of life. Enjoy family-friendly activities throughout the day, including dance performances by Grupo los Tecuanes, making paper marigolds to be placed on a Catrina statue, and making papel picado (perforated paper decorations) with David Amorozo. Learn how pan de muerto (bread of the dead) is made with Neil Vargas, Jr. Learn about La Catrina and her joyful view of life and mortality by interacting with live Catrinas roaming the festival. Visitors are invited to leave photos and mementos of their loved ones on the ofrenda (altar) or commemorate them by writing their names on a butterfly to attach to the memorial arch. SCHEDULE OF EVENTS LEVEL 3: imagiNATIONS Activity Center 10:30 AM | Story Time Families are invited to an interactive story time featuring the book Día de los Muertos by Roseanne Greenfield Thong. They will have the opportunity to engage with objects from the museum's Teaching Collection such as photographs, textiles, or natural materials to deepen their understanding of Día de los Muertos . Tickets may be needed to enter the imagiNATIONS Activity Center and Story Room. Please see staff at the Level 3 entrance desk for assistance. *Recommended for children ages 3-9 and their caregivers. 11 AM–1 PM, 2–4 PM | Hands On: La Catrina Creations! Celebrate the vibrant artistry of Día de los Muertos by decorating a plaster skull from a variety of La Catrina and Calavera (sugar skull) designs. Using paint markers, participants will create a unique keepsake to take home. LEVEL 1: Potomac Atrium 11 AM, 1 PM, 2:30 PM, and 4 PM | Dance Performances by Grupo los Tecuanes The name of the Danza de los Tecuanes (Dance of the Jaguar) is rooted in the Mixtec understanding of the duality of life and death and the fight of good against evil. The Danza de los Viejitos (Dance of the Old Men) is a humorous dance featuring dancers colorfully dressed as old men. The Flor de Piña (Pineapple Flower) is a folk dance from Oaxaca that features women dancing with pineapples balanced on their right shoulders throughout the routine. Each performance will offer bilingual narration. 11 AM-4 PM | Ongoing Activities Hands On: Paper Marigolds Marigolds, or cempasúchitl , serve a special purpose during Día de los Muertos celebrations. Their petals are used to create a path between the cemetery and the family home. Make your own tissue-paper marigold to take home or create a garland to adorn a nine-foot-tall La Catrina , the iconic skeleton fashionista that has become a symbol of Día de los Muertos. Alfombras de Aserrín (Sawdust Carpet) Display with Ubaldo Sanchez (Maya Mam) Found throughout Mexico and Guatemala, alfombras de Asserín were used in celebrations prior to contact with Europeans. Visitors will have intermittent opportunities to join artist Ubaldo Sanchez in creating a sawdust carpet. Demonstrations: Papel Picado with David Amorozo Papel picado is the Indigenous art form of hand-cut and die-cut paper banners that dates back to pre-Hispanic Mexico. The banners were originally made from a type of bark paper called amate . Today, papel picado is made by cutting tissue paper into intricate designs for Día de los Muertos and other celebrations throughout the year. Learn how it's made with demonstrations by artist David Amorozo. Demonstrations: Pan de muerto with Neil Vargas, Jr. Learn how pan de muerto (bread of the dead) is made with Neil Vargas, Jr., This round bread is traditionally eaten during Día de los Muertos , at a loved one’s gravesite or by the ofrenda. The bread is usually a soft, sweet, round bun often spiced with anise seeds, orange zest or orange flower water. Live: La Catrina La Catrina , the iconic skeleton fashionista that has become a symbol of Día de los Muertos shares a joyful view of life and mortality. Interact with live Catrinas throughout the day as they roam the festival. Butterfly Memorial Arch Select a butterfly of your choice, write a loved one’s name or a short message, and attach the butterfly to the memorial arch. Museum Ofrenda This temporary display honors those who have passed on with photographs or personal effects of the deceased accompanied by flowers, candles, religious icons, water, salt, and an array of food and drink.

events.description: Celebrate Diwali , the Hindu festival of lights, by exploring how light can reveal new perspectives on art. events.name: Celebramos a los Veteranos: A Festival of Service and Remembrance
events.description: Across 250 years of American history, generations of Latinos have served the nation through the U.S. military. Celebramos a los Veteranos: A Festival of Service and Remembrance honors that history while bringing together veterans, service members, families and communities to reflect on what it means to serve. Presented by the National Museum of the American Latino at the National Museum of American History, the festival will explore stories of military service across generations—from Admiral David Glasgow Farragut to Colonel Marisol Chalas and veterans serving today. Through conversations with veterans, service members and military historians; historical tributes; a pop-up exhibition; and participation from veterans organizations nationwide, the program will examine the many ways Latino service has shaped American military history. Visitors will also experience the music of military and civic life, exploring how marching bands, patriotic music and other musical traditions have become part of the American soundscape. A special story booth will invite veterans to record their own recollections of military service and reflect on why they served. Presented in collaboration with the American GI Forum, American Latino Veterans Association, Hispanic Veterans Leadership Alliance, and the League of United Latin American Citizens. Should you need assistance such as ASL interpretation, please email NMALeducation@si.edu with your name, date of program, and request and the museum will respond with further information. When possible, we ask for two-week notice.

events.description: Learn more about your place in the world through explorations of nature and culture. Join us Saturday, November 7th, as we celebrate National Bison Day! Discover different bison adaptations and learn how the bison almost went extinct but are now rising in numbers. Families with learners of all ages will be invited to explore different stations, make observations of museum specimens up close, and explore bisons through play and art. This is a drop-in event. Families can drop in anytime from 10:00am - 12:30pm and stay for as long as your family would like. No registration is required. Cost: Free. Location: Meet at the entrace of Q?rius, The Coralyn W. Whitney Science Education Center, on the Ground Floor of the museum. Q?rius is located next to the Constitution Avenue entrance. Accessibility : Access services such as American Sign Language interpretation, real-time captioning (CART), or audio-description are available with advanced notice. However, accommodations may not be possible with less than two-weeks advanced notice. To request this service, please call (202) 633-5238 or e-mail NMNHAccessibility@si.edu . events.name: DC | Service and Sacrifice: Veterans Day 2026
events.description: Join the National Museum of the American Indian in honoring the enduring and distinguished service of Native Americans in every branch of the US military. Throughout the day, visitors of all ages can learn more about Native military service and honor veterans through presentations, a short film, hands-on activities, various information tables, and more. The Native American Women Warriors (NAWW) will present the colors to begin the day's programming with a welcome from museum leadership. Take in the exhibition Why We Serve: Native Americans in the United States Armed Forces and watch the short film that complements the exhibition. Hear about the history and design of the National Native American Veterans Memorial on our grounds. Learn about the significance of tobacco in Indigenous cultures and make prayer ties to honor veterans. Meet with members of the Native American Women Warriors and learn about their service. Color your own Lakota star quilt as you learn about the history and significance of quilts in Plains cultures. Representatives from the Department of Veterans Affairs will be on hand to share information and resources available for veterans and their families. Dr. Christine Sims (Acoma Pueblo), Associate Professor in the Department of Language, Literacy, and Sociocultural Studies in the College of Education & Human Sciences at the University of New Mexico (UNM) will share the stories of Pueblo men who served as Code Talkers in World War II. Ryan S. Flahive , archivist at the Institute of American Indian Arts (IAIA), will discuss the life and legacy of Native fashion designer, co-founder of IAIA, and veteran Lloyd "Kiva" New (Cherokee. 1916-2002). The lighting of the flame of the National Native American Veterans Memorial will feature an Honor Song and drum by Dennis Zotigh (Kiowa/Isanti Dakota/Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo) and Ralph Zotigh (Kiowa/Isanti Dakota/Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo). The Native American Women Warriors will retire the colors to conclude the day's events. Portions of the day’s events (marked with * below) will be livestreamed, watch at AmericanIndian.si.edu/livestream . Full schedule of events to be announced. This program is designed for visitors of all ages, and no prior drawing experience is necessary. Anyone under 18 must be accompanied by an adult. events.name: Spirit Toonz: D.C. Soccer in Art
events.description: Join artist Rain Young for a fun, hands-on art workshop celebrating soccer, creativity, and Washington, D.C.’s ever-evolving story. Participants will choose from a selection of featured Washington Spirit players and create one large collectible sports card using a playful, cartoon-inspired interpretation of their chosen player. With illustration, color, and imagination, families can add their own creative style to a one-of-a-kind card to take home. More than a sports card, each creation offers an opportunity to explore how art and sports can help tell the stories of the people, teams, and moments that have become part of D.C. history. As objects and stories connected to Washington sports rotate through We Make History, the workshop invites families to think about history as something that isn’t only in the past—it’s something we’re all making every day. Whether you love soccer, drawing, collecting sports cards, or simply creating together, come kick off your creativity and make a little D.C. history of your own! All materials will be provided.

events.description: Join a museum educator for a family-friendly interactive tour of the Water's Edge: The Art of Truman Lowe exhibition!
